title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
question: How does sign marking detect a duplicate?
answer: Each value x marks index x-1 negative on its first occurrence. If that slot is already negative when x appears again, x has been seen before and is a duplicate.

title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
question: Why is abs needed when reading values during sign marking?
answer: The marking process mutates values to negative numbers. Taking abs recovers the original value before converting it to an index.

title: String Compression
question: Why are separate read and write pointers used?
answer: The read pointer scans the original runs while the write pointer stores the compressed result in the same array. Since output never grows beyond the consumed input, overwriting is safe.

title: String Compression
question: How are run lengths greater than nine written?
answer: Convert the count to decimal text and write each digit separately after the character. This handles multi-digit run lengths without extra array storage.

title: Add Two Numbers II
question: Why use stacks to add forward-order linked lists?
answer: The least significant digits are at the list tails. Stacks expose those digits first, allowing ordinary right-to-left addition with carry.

title: Add Two Numbers II
question: Why is each result digit prepended to the output list?
answer: Digits are generated from least significant to most significant. Prepending each digit builds the final list in forward order directly.

title: Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
question: What does dp[i][diff] count?
answer: It counts arithmetic subsequences of length at least two that end at index i with the given difference. Each such sequence can be extended by a later matching value.

title: Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
question: Why is only the existing sequence count added to the answer?
answer: Every existing length-at-least-two sequence extended by the current value becomes a valid length-at-least-three sequence. The new pair itself is stored in DP but is not counted yet.

title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
question: How do positive slots identify missing values?
answer: Each present value marks the slot indexed by value-1 negative. Any slot that remains positive corresponds to a value that never appeared.

title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
question: Does in-place marking require extra memory proportional to n?
answer: No. The algorithm uses the input array's signs as markers and stores only the output list, so its auxiliary space is constant excluding output.

title: Delete Node in a BST
question: How is a BST node with two children deleted?
answer: Replace its value with the smallest value in its right subtree, then recursively delete that inorder successor from the right subtree.

title: Delete Node in a BST
question: Why is the inorder successor safe to copy into the deleted node?
answer: It is the smallest value larger than the node's left subtree and no greater than other values in the right subtree, so replacing the node preserves BST ordering.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
question: Why is frequency counting followed by sorting sufficient?
answer: The output only requires characters grouped by descending count. Counting distinct characters and sorting those entries determines the output order, after which each character is repeated by its count.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
question: What is the time complexity when u distinct characters occur in a string of length n?
answer: Counting and output construction are O(n); sorting the u distinct characters costs O(u log u), for O(n+u log u) total.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
question: Why choose the earliest interval end for the next arrow?
answer: The earliest end is the most restrictive interval endpoint. Placing an arrow there bursts that interval and every later interval containing that point, leaving maximum room for remaining balloons.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
question: Why does start > end trigger a new arrow rather than start >= end?
answer: Balloon intervals include their endpoints. An arrow at the previous end also bursts an interval starting exactly there, so a new arrow is needed only when start is strictly greater.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements
question: Why is incrementing n-1 elements equivalent to decrementing one element?
answer: Adding one to all but one element increases their relative values exactly as if the excluded element had been decreased by one. Repeating this makes the minimum element the target.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements
question: What formula gives the minimum number of moves?
answer: If m is the minimum array value, the answer is the sum over all elements of value-m.

title: 4Sum II
question: Why count pair sums from only two arrays?
answer: The equation a+b+c+d=0 can be rearranged as a+b=-(c+d). A frequency map for the first pair lets every second-pair sum contribute its matching number of index combinations.

title: 4Sum II
question: Why use a long accumulator for the quadruple count?
answer: There can be many index combinations even when array values are small. The total count may exceed the range of intermediate pair-sum counts, so a wide accumulator avoids overflow.
